sections.heading: Belief vs. doubt
sections.body:
- **Believing, thinking, being sure → indicative**: *Creo que tienes razón. Pienso que es buena idea. Estoy seguro de que viene. Me parece que está cerrado.*
- **Doubting or denying → subjunctive**: *Dudo que venga.* (I doubt he's coming.) *No creo que tengas razón.* (I don't think you're right.) *No pienso que sea buena idea. No estoy seguro de que funcione. No me parece que esté cerrado.*

The negative flips the mood: *Creo que es verdad* (indicative) → *No creo que sea verdad* (subjunctive). And *dudar* flips the other way: *No dudo que es verdad* (indicative — you don't doubt it, so you believe it).

sections.heading: Maybe, perhaps
sections.body:
- *Quizás / Quizá / Tal vez* + subjunctive when you're unsure: *Quizás llueva mañana. Tal vez tengas razón.* (They can also take the indicative when you feel more confident — both are heard.)
- *A lo mejor* + **indicative** always: *A lo mejor llueve mañana.* (Very common in speech.)
- *Puede (ser) que* + subjunctive: *Puede que no venga.* (He might not come.)
- *Seguramente / probablemente* + indicative (usually): *Seguramente llega tarde.*

sections.heading: Asking about beliefs
sections.body: In questions, *¿Crees que…?* usually takes the indicative when you're genuinely asking: *¿Crees que va a llover?* Using the subjunctive (*¿Crees que llueva?*) signals more doubt — it's common in Latin American speech.

examples: No estoy seguro de que funcione.
I'm not sure it will work.
No me parece que esté cerrado.
No pienso que sea buena idea.
I don't think it's a good idea.
Do you think it's going to rain?
We doubt they can finish today.
